analysis.one_liner: Lets struggling student loan borrowers erase their debt in bankruptcy under a plain "hardship" standard instead of the nearly impossible "undue hardship" test.
analysis.headline: The bill to let student borrowers erase their loans through bankruptcy, like credit card and medical debt, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on July 16, 2025 and has not moved since.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, student loans are the only major consumer debt that cannot be wiped out in bankruptcy unless a borrower proves "undue hardship" — a standard so strict that fewer than one in a thousand who even try succeed. This bill deletes the word "undue" from the bankruptcy code, letting courts use an ordinary "hardship" standard, with the normal bankruptcy safeguards (means testing, disclosure, exemptions) still applying. It would apply to cases already filed as well as future ones.
analysis.who_benefits: Struggling student loan borrowers — currently about 43 million federal borrowers, with roughly 20% in default and an estimated 10 million heading toward default — who would finally be able to seek the same fresh start in bankruptcy available to people with credit card or medical debt [S2]. Court records show only about 2,500 borrowers even attempted a discharge between November 2022 and September 2024, because attorneys discourage clients from trying [S2].

how_it_helps.text: A borrower who genuinely cannot pay would be able to have student loans wiped out in bankruptcy court under a plain 'hardship' standard, the same way other consumer debts are treated.

Courts would regain flexibility to set reasonable criteria, replacing the Brunner test, which most courts use and which the bill's findings say has produced successful discharges for fewer than 0.1% of the borrowers who even try.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government (and ultimately taxpayers) would absorb more loan balances written off in bankruptcy; private and federal lenders would price in higher losses, which could mean higher rates for future borrowers [S2].

drawbacks.text: Critics have long worried that making student loans dischargeable invites borrowers to file bankruptcy right after graduation and shift those costs to taxpayers or future students, a concern the bill's own findings argue was already addressed by the 2005 means test but which remains the standard objection.

The bill applies retroactively to cases already filed and pending, which lenders and guarantors could argue upsets expectations in active proceedings and adds unpredictability to the value of existing loan portfolios.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large for a specific group: borrowers with no realistic ability to repay, who today almost never qualify for relief. The cost falls on the federal loan program (and ultimately taxpayers) for debts written off, and the bill offers no compromise for concerns about moral hazard, though the bill text points out that means testing and all other bankruptcy safeguards would still apply. For those borrowers, the change would be the difference between a lifetime of garnished wages and a fresh start.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee in July 2025, and no committee hearing, vote, or floor action has happened since.

narrative.text: The only action taken was the July 16, 2025 introduction and referral to the House Judiciary Committee; the bill has received no further action since.
Support is entirely Democratic: the sponsor and all 24 cosponsors are House Democrats, and no House Republican has signed on in a chamber where Republicans hold 223 of 440 seats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo is preserved: federal and private student lenders keep the special protection that makes their loans nearly impossible to erase, and borrowers remain stuck with debts they cannot pay.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Student lenders and the loan status quo

for.name: Rep. J. Luis Correa
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its findings documenting that fewer than 0.1% of student loan discharge attempts succeed.

for.name: 24 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor is a Democrat.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was referred on July 16, 2025 — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controls the House floor agenda and has shown no interest in bringing student-debt relief measures to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 supporters are House Democrats; with Republicans holding 223 of 440 House seats and no Republican cosponsors, the bill has no path without majority-party action.

industries.industry: Federal student loan program / U.S. Department of Education
industries.note: Debts currently uncollectible could be discharged, reducing amounts the federal government expects to recover, but discharge converts some never-paid balances into partial repayment plans inside bankruptcy.
Private student loans, which today enjoy the same near-impossible discharge standard, would become dischargeable, raising lenders' risk and likely raising rates for future borrowers.
The bill's findings note attorneys currently discourage clients from even trying to discharge student loans; a fairer standard would create work that was previously seen as pointless.

analysis.trajectory: A one-line amendment sitting in the House Judiciary Committee with no Republican support and no action in months is very unlikely to advance this Congress; unless it gains bipartisan sponsors or gets folded into a larger bankruptcy or higher-education bill, it will likely die quietly when the session ends.
